extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and legal scholars working on U.S. patent infringement issues
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts substantive legal standards for what constitutes infringement of a U.S. patent (making, using, selling, marking, notice, timing, and secondary liability), with explanatory guidance and case examples useful for advising, pleading, litigating, or deciding infringement claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral acts not per se infringement (possession/exposure/advertising)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere possession of a patented invention, its exposure for sale, exhibition to others, advertising, and similar collateral acts, taken alone, do not constitute an infringement though they may raise a strong presumption of invasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These collateral acts are evidence that infringement may have occurred but do not by themselves disturb the patentee's rights; examples/cases: Minter v. Williams (1835), Allis v. Stowell (1881) (advertising is not per se infringement but is strong evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement must relate to the precise invention claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of manufacture, use, or sale must relate to the precise invention as claimed; the accused product/process must be identical in effect, function, and mode of operation to the claimed invention to constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent exceptions for machine patents (where employing the structural law may appropriate the whole idea) are in reality applications of the requirement that the accused thing embody the essential structure/idea; see sections and cases referenced regarding machine patents and equivalents (§900 and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using part of a patented invention is not infringement unless it appropriates the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing a distinct part of a patented invention is not an infringement unless that part itself constitutes an infringement or is an essential/operative equivalent of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the part used embodies the essential parts or equivalents of the claimed invention or, in machines, embraces the complete expression of the structural law, use may be infringement; see Sessions v. Romadka (1884) and related notes (§900, §926).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention of actor generally immaterial to infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, the mental intention with which an act is performed is immaterial: infringement occurs whether or not the actor intended to violate the patent or even knew of the patent's existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, where external acts are equivocal, the actor's intent may be an element converting otherwise innocent conduct into an infringement (analogous to specific intent in criminal law); see Parker v. Hulme (1849) and related discussion (§901).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent marking/notice obligation to prevent ignorant infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The law imposes on the patentee an obligation to notify the public of their claims (e.g., stamping 'patented' with the patent date on the article or its package); failure to mark may bar recovery of substantial damages against persons not otherwise notified of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For functional arts the patent specification discloses practice; for tangible articles, marking allows the public to learn the invention from the article itself. See statutory/duty-to-stamp discussion and cases referenced (§902/Infringement through Ignorance').

rubrics_metrics.name: Making: when manufacture constitutes infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'make' a patented article includes construction or repairs amounting to reconstruction; making is complete when the article exists in condition fit for use. Making for practical use or for sale is infringement; making for mere experiment or exhibition is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key distinctions: experimental or exhibition making is not infringement (Standard Measuring Machine Co. v. Teague (1888), Poppenhusen v. Falke (1861)). Making a single part with intent to unite it to others or making a different article intended to become the patented article is infringement. Repairs that reconstruct the article may be infringement (Goodyear Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Perrin, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency/outsourced making is still making (primary liability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a patented article by the agency of others (workmen, co-partners) is an act of making by the principal and constitutes infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where maker pays by piece and delivers completed articles, the principal-maker is liable; examples and citations are given in the treatise (§903 and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use: experimental use exception versus beneficial use infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a patented art or article solely for experiment is not infringement; employing it for any beneficial or pecuniary object is infringement, regardless of whether the article was purchased or altered after manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alterations, division into parts, or new uses/improvements do not absolve infringement; using a device in an altered condition, or using essential features or equivalents, is infringement (Illinois Central R.R. v. Turnill; Sessions v. Romadka). Use by a purchaser may be restricted if an injunction is in place or if purchaser acts in complicity with infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial use or provision to others can be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Using part of an invention with intent that others complete the operation, or using through agents who provide finished results, constitutes infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplying parts or intermediate results enabling others to complete the patented process or product can create liability; the treatise cites continuations of infringement via agency and instances where providing the finished output by others still amounts to infringing use (§904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of equivalents and essential features is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the essential features of the invention or their equivalents constitutes infringement even if the accused device varies in number or appearance of parts so long as it performs the same function or embodies the essential idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Sessions v. Romadka (1884); Yale Lock Mfg. Co. v. Norwich National Bank (1881) (use of an equivalent may infringe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using for a new/unanticipated purpose may still infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a patented device for a purpose not specified or contemplated by the inventor can still be infringement if it employs the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise cites Cincinnati Ice Mach. Co. v. Foss-Schneider Brewing Co. (1887) and other examples where new uses of the invention were held infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling without authority is always infringement; sale definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Selling a patented article without the patentee's authority is always infringement. 'Sale' for patent law purposes includes any transfer that passes apparent title or ownership (including disguised transfers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any transfer that effectively passes ownership/possession for value may be a 'sale' under the Patent Laws (see §905 and notes). Sale of a part intended to be united with other parts to create the patented article, or sale of a different article intended to become the patented article, can be infringement. However, sales under legal process (e.g., sheriff's sale) or sales of articles where patent covers 'use' (not sale) may have distinct consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of parts/materials: conditional infringement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of a part of an article may not infringe a different patent covering the whole unless the seller intends or knows the part will be used to infringe; sale of materials ready to be united and used may not ipso facto be infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selling a part covered by one patent does not automatically infringe another patent covering the whole (Keystone Bridge Co. v. Phoenix Iron Co.). But selling materials with directions or knowledge that they will be used to infringe, or selling in collusion with infringing makers/users, creates liability (Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. American Zylonite Co.; Snyder v. Bunnell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary/joint liability for sales or transport with infringing intent
rubrics_metrics.description: A seller who knowingly supplies materials or transports devices for use in infringement, or who sells with directions that enable copying the patented invention, is a joint or contributory infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. American Zylonite Co.; American Cotton Tie Supply Co. v. McCready. Acts of complicity must be proved as to both act and intent; mere capability of infringing use alone is insufficient without evidence of intent or participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colorable contracts and arrangements to procure infringing manufacture can be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangements that are in form a contract but in substance procure infringing manufacture or use (e.g., a sham contract to take infringing output for the benefit of the procurer) can make the procurer an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Keplinger v. De Young (1825) and discussion—substance over form; leasing and complicit use may join lessor and lessee as joint infringers (Wells v. Jaques).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale by licensee or sale where patentee authorized manufacturing/selling is not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale authorized by the patentee or his licensee is not infringement; similarly, the patentee's licensing of makers who apply may prevent infringement liability for those makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the patentee has agreed to license all who apply, manufacture and sale by licensees are not infringing (Saxe v. Hammond (1875) and related notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of making/use/sale by different persons can be jointly actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one party makes and another sells or uses the same infringing machine or process, they may be jointly and severally liable as infringers, though multiple acts can constitute one cause of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jennings v. Dolan (1887). The treatise notes that making by one and use or sale by another are essentially distinct acts but may be treated as parts of the same wrong for remedies; evidence of complicity is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement is a single tort regardless of multiple infringing acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Although making, using, and selling are each independent acts that can constitute infringement, when the same person performs two or more of these acts they constitute a single tort and a single cause of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple acts do not multiply liability as separate causes of action; they may affect measure of damages, injunctive relief, and accounting but are one wrong (Steam Stone Cutter Co. v. Sheldon and discussion §906).

rubrics_metrics.name: No infringement can occur before patent issue (timing rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: An act cannot be infringement of a patent unless it is performed during the life of the patent; acts before the patent issues, while potentially tortious, are not 'infringement' under the patent privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under U.S. law, the patent's creation (issue) is the earliest point when the privilege exists and infringement can occur; English courts sometimes treat post-filing/pre-sealing conduct differently, but U.S. rule requires issuance. Re-issues are considered new patents and likewise cannot be infringed before they are granted; see cases like Lyon v. Donaldson, and discussion (§907).

rubrics_metrics.name: No infringement after patent expiration (term limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, infringement cannot be committed after the patent term has expired; infringing acts must occur during the patent's grant term (including any extension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Termination of the exclusive privilege ends liability; the treatise notes this general rule and that remedies for pre-issue or other hardships are left to legislative correction (discussion in §906/§907 area).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and limitation when marking/notice is absent
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to mark patented articles may limit patentee's recovery of damages against persons who lacked actual notice of the patent, though other remedies (e.g., injunction) may still exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee's duty to mark and the statutory consequences of failing to mark are discussed; see Allen v. Deacon (1884) and §628 notes for duties and effects of stamping. The treatise emphasizes the public-notice rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair versus reconstruction: replacement of parts may constitute infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing or repairing parts of a patented machine can constitute infringement if the repair amounts to reconstruction of the patented article (making rather than permissible repair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where replacement goes beyond ordinary repair into reconstruction of the patented device, liability follows (Singer Mfg. Co. v. Springfield Foundry Co.; Graham v. Mason (1872) and related citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser's rights limited during injunctions or pending suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser from an alleged infringer cannot use the device without infringing if an injunction against the seller/inventor forbids such use; purchasers may be enjoined or liable depending on timing and notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases illustrate that purchasers may be prevented from using devices pending injunctions or in the face of notice (Woodworth v. Edwards, and related discussion).
